rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anqada denotes a creaking or cracking sound; the usage extends beyond loads and men to joints, whose sounds make the back creak under a heavy burden.
rows.anchor: وهو صوت الانتقاض والانفكاك أعني الصرير ولا يختص بصوت المحامل والرجال بل يضاف إلى المفاصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abbas ibn Mirdas uses anqada for a back creaking under strain from those for whom he felt concern, illustrating the word's bodily image.
rows.anchor: وأنقض ظهري ما تطويت منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attributing the creaking to the burden is a metaphorical attribution of an effect to its cause; the burden itself is the cause being carried.
rows.anchor: وإسناد الانقاض للحمل إسناد للسبب الحامل مجازاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One proposed burden is something the Prophet did before his mission that later weighed on him; its removal would mean forgiveness.
rows.anchor: ما صدر منه صلى الله عليه وسلم قبل البعثة مما يشق عليه صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another proposal is his lack of revealed knowledge of religious laws despite seeking them; removal means teaching him through revelation.
rows.anchor: أو غفلته عن الشرائع ونحوها مما لا يدرك إلا بالوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be his perplexity about matters such as fulfilling the mission or receiving revelation; its removal resolves that perplexity.
rows.anchor: أو حيرته عليه الصلاة والسلام في بعض الأمور كأداء حق الرسالة أو الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be how extremely difficult the mission and revelation initially felt; removal is their easing through practice and habituation.
rows.anchor: فقد كان يثقل عليه صلى الله عليه وسلم في ابتداء أمره جداً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be seeing his people astray while unable to guide them because they would not obey or accept truth; its removal includes God guiding some, such as Hamza and Umar, to Islam.
rows.anchor: ما كان يرى صلى الله عليه وسلم من ضلال قومه مع العجز عن إرشادهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The burden may be witnessing his people's transgressions in harming him; its removal is strengthening him to endure them.
rows.anchor: أو ما كان يرى من تعديهم في إيذائه عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the sūra came after Abu Talib and Khadija died, the burden may be grief for them; removal is consolation through ascension, angels' greeting, and beholding his greatest beloved and Lord.
rows.anchor: بناء على نزول الصورة بعد وفاتهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Across these proposed meanings, the verse uses an extended illustrative metaphor, with placing the burden serving as a reinforcing extension of the image.
rows.anchor: ففي الكلام استعارة تمثيلية والوضع ترشيح لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says this wording does not establish the author's position on prophetic impeccability.
rows.anchor: وليس فيه دليل لنا في العصمة كما لا يخفى

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan chooses to read placing the burden as figuratively expressing the Prophet's protection from sins and purification from impurities, hyperbolically denying such faults.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو حيان كون وضع الوزر كتابة عن عصمته

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Some say the burden is the community's, attributed to the Prophet because of his concern for it; its removal lifts worldly punishment while he remains among them and they seek forgiveness. Al-Ālūsī considers this remote.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد وزر أمتك وإنما أضيف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community-burden interpretation invokes the promise that God would not punish them while the Prophet was among them or while they sought forgiveness.
rows.anchor: ما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas is reported to have read the phrase with the verbs حططنا and حللنا in place of وضعنا.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أنس وحططنا وحللنا مكان وضعنا

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's variant reads وحللنا عنك وقرك in place of the standard wording.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود وحللنا عنك وقرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God elevated the Prophet's remembrance through prophethood and many other ways: his name paired with God's in the testimony, obedience to him paired with obedience to God, blessings on him, honored divine forms of address, and mention in earlier scriptures and covenants.
rows.anchor: بالنبوة وغيرها وأي رفع مثل أن قرن اسمه عليه الصلاة والسلام باسمه عز وجل في كلمتي الشهادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة ومحمد بن كعب والضحاك والحسن
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, Muhammad ibn Kab, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, and others explain that the Prophet is never mentioned without being mentioned alongside God.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد وقتادة ومحمد بن كعب والضحاك والحسن وغيرهم أنهم قالوا في ذلك لا أذكر إلا ذكرت معي

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Said al-Khudri reports a Prophetic account: Gabriel conveyed God's question about the raised remembrance; God answered that whenever He is mentioned, the Prophet is mentioned with Him. No grading is given.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سعيد الخدري عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report's focus on mention alongside God selects the greatest instance among the many ways remembrance was raised; Hassan's verses illustrate the pairing in the call to prayer.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك من الاقتصار على ما هو أعظم قدراً من أفراد رفع الذكر

rows.speaker: حسان
rows.claim: Hassan's cited poetry says God joined the Prophet's name to His own, so the caller testifies to both at each of the five prayers.
rows.anchor: وضم الاله اسم النبي إلى اسمه إذا قال في الخمس المؤذن أشهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī notes the subtle sequence of raising remembrance after placing the burden, along with the conjunction and the added لك, discussed as before.
rows.anchor: ولا يخفى لطف ذكر الرفع بعد الوضع والكلام في العطف وزيادة لك كالذي سلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated sentence could reinforce the first, but Al-Ālūsī prefers a fresh promise: establishing a new assurance is more eloquent than mere confirmation, especially in this consoling context.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون تكريراً للجملة السابقة لتقرير معناها وفي النفوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the fresh-promise reading, the ease may mean relief available in the caliphs' days or ease in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: بيد أن المراد باليسر هنا ما تيسر لهم في أيام الخلفاء أو يسر الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fresh-promise analysis is a syntactic resumption; such separation without waw is common, so no special explanation for the missing conjunction is needed.
rows.anchor: واحتمال الاستئناف هو الراجح لما علم من فضل التأسيس على التأكيد

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: Isam al-Din suggests that separation may be artful because the independent clause takes the form of a repetition; Al-Ālūsī answers that resumption already accounts for it.
rows.anchor: وقال عصام الدين لا يبعد أن تكون نكتة الفصل كونه في صورة التكرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite noun is used for magnification; it may also signal a new assurance, since repeating an indefinite suggests a different instance and contrast between hardship and ease.
rows.anchor: إلا أنه أوثر التنكير التفخيم وقد يقال إن فائدته الظهور في التأسيس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports that the Prophet came out delighted and laughing, saying one hardship would not overcome two eases, then recited these assurances. No grading is given.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن قال خرج رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فرحاً مسروراً وهو يضحك ويقول لن يغلب عسر يسرين

rows.speaker: بعض الأجلة
rows.claim: A scholar says the clause confirms the preceding blessings and promises the Prophet that every difficulty will be made easy.
rows.anchor: وأفاد بعض الأجلة أن الكلام تقرير لما قبله وعدة له صلى الله عليه وسلم بتيسير كل عسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this explanation, fa is causal though it precedes the cause: mentioning either hardship or ease calls the other to mind; the definite article generalizes hardship and the indefinite ease is magnified.
rows.anchor: فالفاء قيل سيبية ودخلت على السبب وان تعارف دخولها على المسبب لتسبب ذكره عن ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic hardship includes distress such as constricted breast, the burden, and obscurity; corresponding great ease includes expansion, relief, and raised remembrance, so one should not despair of God's relief.
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل فعلنا لك كذا وكذا لأن مع كل عسر كضيق الصدر والوزر المنقض للظهر والخمول

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another commentator takes fa as inferential, deriving a general rule from particular cases, like inferring that all animals move the lower jaw because humans, horses, and sheep do so when chewing.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم الفاء للتفريع وهو من قبيل تفريع الحكم على الدليل في صورة الاستدلال بالجزئي على الكلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second sentence has the same alternatives, and a fresh promise remains preferable; if hardship is one while ease is reiterated, the two great eases apparently mean worldly and afterlife relief.
rows.anchor: وفي الجملة الثانية الاحتمالان السابقان والاستئناف أيضاً هو الراجح لما تقدم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the second sentence as repetition for emphasis, with the same hardship and ease both times, like repeating that a horseman has a spear.
rows.anchor: وقيل الظاهر أن الجملة الثانية تكرير للأولى وتأكيد لها فاليسر فيها عين اليسر في الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying about one hardship and two eases does not prove a distinct second promise: emphatic repetition can magnify one ease until it encompasses relief in both worlds.
rows.anchor: ولن يغلب عسر يسرين ليس نصاً في الحمل على الاستئناف إذ يصح على التأكيد أيضاً

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The second sentence is absent from Ibn Masud's codex, although the saying about one hardship and two eases is also transmitted from him; this weakens the claim that the saying proves two distinct eases.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس في مصحف ابن مسعود الجملة الثانية مع أنه جاء عنه أيضاً لن يغلب عسر يسرين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further proposal says one hardship cannot overcome the ease mentioned twice in a consoling promise; Al-Ālūsī dismisses this construal as strained.
rows.anchor: وقيل يمكن أن يحمل الخبر على أنه لن يغلب فرد من أفراد العسر ذكر اليسر مرتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The familiar explanation treats maʿa, accompaniment, as a metaphor for baʿda, after: their closeness exaggerates how promptly ease follows hardship.
rows.anchor: والمشهور على جميع الأوجه أنه شبه التقارب بالتقارن فاستعير لفظ مع لمعنى بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Generic hardship seems problematic because lasting illness or poverty may have no worldly sequel, and a disbeliever's hardship may have no afterlife ease; the consoling judgment is understood for believers.
rows.anchor: واستشكل أمر الاستغراق بأن من العسر ما لا يعقبه يسر دنيوي كالفقر والمرض الدائمين إلى الموت

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam reports that Abu Ubayda wrote Umar about Roman forces; Umar replied that distress falling on a believer is followed by relief. Al-Ālūsī says the report does not resolve every case.
rows.anchor: ما رواه مالك في الموطأ عن زيد بن أسلم قال كتب أبو عبيدة إلى عمر بن الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even restricting the promise to believers leaves hardships without worldly relief, and an impatient believer may receive no afterlife reward; a patient-only reading still leaves difficulty.
rows.anchor: إذ يبقى معه إن من عسر المؤمن ما لا يعقبه يسر دنيوي كما هو ظاهر

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: On the emphatic reading, some answer that generic scope is conventional and hardship is usually followed by ease; on a fresh-promise reading, they add that it concerns a patient believer.
rows.anchor: وأجاب بعض على وجه التأكيد بأن الاستغراق عرفي ويكفي فيه أن العسر في الغالب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reports that the Prophet told his companions that two hardships would not overcome two eases, God willing; this supplies a condition not explicit in the verse.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في الآية قال ذكر لنا أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بهذه الآية أصحابه

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: Some allow literal accompaniment: every hardship has at least some ease, such as God's averting something worse; magnified ease is prevention of greater harm.
rows.anchor: يفهم من كلام بعض الأفاضل أنه يجوز على وجه التأكيد أن يكون مع على ظاهرها

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: Under literal accompaniment, the two eases may be one ease mentioned twice or immediate assurance plus customary later relief; the argument may also invoke 65:7 if revealed earlier.
rows.anchor: وأنه لا يأبى ذلك لن يغلب عسر يسرين اما لأن المعنى لن يغلب فرد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some elect mystics say accompaniment is literal because everything the Beloved does is beloved; Ibn al-Farid and an anonymous Persian poet depict lovers savoring harsh treatment. Al-Ālūsī rejects this.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعضم ان المعية على حقيقتها عند الخاصة على معنى ان كل ما فعل المحبوب محبوب

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet said ease would enter a stone to drive hardship out, then recited the verse; Al-Ālūsī says this makes literal accompaniment unlikely. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم جالساً وحياله حجر فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام لو جاء العسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading al-ʿusr as a known hardship avoids objections and suits the occasion report, but the apparent rhetoric favors generality; then the promise is conditioned on trust, hope, and reliance on God.
rows.anchor: وإرادة العهد أسلم من القيل والقال وكأن من اختاره اختاره لذلك مع الاستئناس له بسبب النزول

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب وأبو جعفر وعيسى
rows.claim: Ibn Waththab, Abu Jafar, and Isa read al-ʿusr and yusran in both occurrences with a damma on the sīn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب وأبو جعفر وعيسى العسر ويسرا في الموضعين بضم السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the Prophet finishes one act of worship, such as conveying revelation, he should exert himself in another as thanks for past blessings and promised favors, leaving no time without worship.
rows.anchor: فاتعب في عبادة أخرى شكراً لما عددنا عليك من النعم السالفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Direct longing and requests to the Lord alone, asking no one else, since He alone can grant what is sought.
rows.anchor: فاحرص بالسؤال ولا تسأل غيره تعالى فإنه القادر على الاسعاف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says that after finishing prayer, one should exert oneself in supplication; al-Dahhak and Qatada are also reported similarly.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قال أي إذا فرغت من لصلاة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says that after finishing obligatory prayers, one should exert oneself in night prayer.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود أي إذا فرغت من الفرائض

rows.speaker: الحسن وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets finishing as completing a campaign, followed by striving in worship; Zayd ibn Aslam is reported to share this view.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن أي إذا فرغت من الغزو فاجتهد في العبادة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says that when one finishes personal or worldly affairs, one should pray; another report from him resembles Ibn Abbas's interpretation.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أي إذا فرغت من أسباب نفسك وفي لقظ من دنياك فصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the general reading of finishing one worship and beginning another; the named practices specify examples, not limits on the verse.
rows.anchor: والأنسب حمل الآية على ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The instruction implies devoting one's time to worship or turning to it after worldly work; idleness or irrelevant occupation shows foolish judgment and heedlessness.
rows.anchor: أن اللائق بحال العبد أن يستغرق أوقاته بالعبادة أو بأن يفرغ إلى العبادة

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar says he dislikes seeing anyone idle and without useful work for worldly or afterlife concerns.
rows.anchor: أني لأكره أن أرى أحدكم فارغاً سبهللا لا في عمل دنياه ولا في عمل آخرته

rows.speaker: شريك
rows.claim: Sharik reportedly saw two men wrestling and asked what had happened to these idle men, illustrating the censure of useless idleness.
rows.anchor: فقال ما بهدا أمر الفارغ

rows.speaker: أبو السمال
rows.claim: Abu al-Sammal reads faraghta with kasra on the rā, a dialect form that al-Zamakhshari calls inelegant.
rows.anchor: فرغت بكسر الراء وهي لغة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: A group reads fansab with a doubled, open bā, from inṣibāb; the meaning is to turn wholly toward another worship.
rows.anchor: بشد الباء مفتوحة من الانصباب والمراد فتوجه إلى عبادة

rows.speaker: بعض الإمامية
rows.claim: A reading attributed to some Imamiyya has fansib with kasra on ṣād and takes the object as Ali: after prophethood, appoint him to the imamate.
rows.anchor: انه قرأ فانصب بكسر الصاد فقيل أي فإذا فرغت من النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī notes that the verse names no particular object to appoint, so a Sunni could equally supply Abu Bakr; the verse alone does not establish the Imamiyya claim.
rows.anchor: ليس في الآية دليل على خصوصية المفعول فللسنى أن يقدره أبا بكر

rows.speaker: السني
rows.claim: In response to the Imamiyya appeal to Ghadir Khumm, the Sunni denies that it proves appointment or is authentic as transmitted by the Imamiyya.
rows.anchor: منع السني دلالته على ما ثبت عنده على النصب وصحته

rows.speaker: السني
rows.claim: The Sunni supports appointing Abu Bakr with the Prophet's instruction that he lead people in prayer, which better fits the completion of his mission in the final illness.
rows.anchor: فللسنى أن يقدره أبا بكر رضي الله تعالى عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Imamiyya reply that the verse means finishing pilgrimage and appointing Ali, Al-Ālūsī objects that the sūra is Meccan.
rows.anchor: ورد عليه أمر مكية السورة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues that if the Imamiyya reading were sound, an anti-Ali partisan could read it as an order to hate Ali; Al-Ālūsī finds this objection flawed.
rows.anchor: وقال في الكشاف لو صح ذلك للرافضي لصح للناصبي

rows.speaker: بعض الناس
rows.claim: Others supply khalīfa, caliph, as the omitted object; Al-Ālūsī says little turns on this proposal.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من قدر المفعول خليفة والأمر فيه هين

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls the Imamiyya reading anomalous and weak in meaning, and says it has not been established from a scholar.
rows.anchor: أن هذه القراءة شاذة ضعيفة المعنى لم تثبت عن عالم

rows.speaker: عصام الدين
rows.claim: Isam al-Din proposes finishing one ease and exerting under another hardship to seek two eases, then aspiring to God; Al-Ālūsī rejects this as contrary to the plain sense.
rows.anchor: وقال عصام الدين لا نسب ان يراد فإذا فرغت من يسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's saying about returning from the lesser to the greater jihad is invoked for Hasan's interpretation, but its fit is questioned because the sūra is Meccan and jihad followed migration; a Medinan sūra or verse, or delayed ruling, could be posited.
rows.anchor: وهو قريب إلا أنه قيل عليه أن السورة مكية والأمر بالجهاد بعد الهجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujahid's worldly-affairs interpretation fits the common use of farāgh for release from worldly occupations and the saying to use free time before busyness, but is the weakest because context and fa point elsewhere.
rows.anchor: أن الفراغ أكثر ما يستعمل في الخلو عن الأشغال الدنيوية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The causal fa favors the general reading that each completed worship is followed by another.
rows.anchor: وهو أضعف الأقوال لبعده عما يقتضيه السياق وتؤذن به الفاء

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي وابن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Ali and Ibn Abi Abla read faraghib, an imperative from the doubled verb raghiba, meaning to urge people to seek what God has.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي وابن أبي عبلة فرغب أمر من رغب بشد الغين

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The saying 'we returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad' is cited in connection with al-Hasan's reading; the source notes the chronology problem but reports possible answers.
rows.anchor: رجعنا من الجهاد الأصغر إلى الجهاد الأكبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isam al-Din's expanded proposal says not to bear worldly hardship for two worldly eases, but to bear hardship seeking the Lord and nearness for both eases; Al-Ālūsī says no sound mind derives this from the wording.
rows.anchor: لا تتحمل عسر الدنيا طمعاً في يسرين فيها بل تحمل عسر طلب الرب وقربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra is also called al-Qiyāma, al-Balad, al-Munfakkin, al-Bariyya, and Lam Yakun, as well as al-Bayyina.
rows.anchor: وتسمى سورة القيامة وسورة البلد وسورة المنفكين وسورة البرية وسورة لم يكن

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Al-Bahr reports that the majority consider the sūra Meccan.
rows.anchor: قال في البحر مكية في قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن الزبير وعطاء بن يسار
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr and Ata ibn Yasar are reported by Ibn Atiyya to consider the sūra Medinan.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الزبير وعطاء بن يسار مدنية قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: كتاب التحرير
rows.claim: Kitab al-Tahrir calls the sūra Medinan and says this is the majority position, contrary to Al-Bahr's report of a Meccan majority.
rows.anchor: وفي كتاب التحرير مدنية وهو قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Abu Salih transmits from Ibn Abbas that the sūra is Meccan; Yahya ibn Sallam chooses that view.
rows.anchor: وروي أبو صالح عن ابن عباس أنها مكية واختاره يحيى بن سلام

rows.speaker: ابن الفرس
rows.claim: Ibn al-Faris says the more widely known position is that the sūra is Meccan; Ibn Mardawayh also transmits this from Aisha.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الفرس الأشهر إنها مكية ورواه ابن مردويه عن عائشة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir decisively considers the sūra Medinan, citing the report that Gabriel instructed the Prophet to recite it to Ubayy ibn Kab.
rows.anchor: وجزم ابن كثير بأنها مدنية واستدل على ذلك بما أخرجه الإمام أحمد

rows.speaker: أبو خيثمة البدري
rows.claim: Abu Khaythama al-Badri reports that Gabriel told the Prophet God commanded him to recite the sūra to Ubayy; Ubayy asked if named, heard yes, and wept. Al-Ālūsī calls this sounder. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن أبي خيثمة البدري قال لما نزلت لم يكن الذين كفروا من أهل الكتاب إلى آخرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra has nine verses in the Basran count and eight in other verse-counting traditions.
rows.anchor: وآيها تسع في البصري وثمان في غيره

rows.speaker: مطر المزني أو المدني
rows.claim: Matar al-Muzani, or al-Madani, transmits a Prophetic merit report: God hears this sūra's recitation and promises reward and a place in Paradise until contentment. No grading is stated.
rows.anchor: عن مطر المزني أو المدني عن النبي صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم قال إن الله تعالى يسمع قراءة لم يكن الذين كفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening explains the Qur'an's revelation: the disbelievers would not desist until the Messenger came reciting purified pages, which is what was revealed.
rows.anchor: إن قوله تعالى فيها لم يكن الذين الخ كالتعليل لإنزال القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahl al-Kitab means Jews and Christians; the title either stresses the enormity of their unbelief or hints that they should follow truth found in their scriptures.
rows.anchor: أي اليهود والنصارى وإيرادهم بذلك العنوان قيل لإعظام شناعة كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause uses a past verb because their unbelief arose after their prophets, through later deviations concerning God's attributes.
rows.anchor: وإيراد الصلة فعلاً لما أن كفرهم حادث بعد أنبيائهم عليهم السلام بالآحاد

rows.speaker: أبو منصور الماتريدي
rows.claim: Abu Mansur al-Maturidi takes min as partitive, not explanatory: some people of the Book remained in true belief until death; explanatory min would imply all disbelieved before the mission.
rows.anchor: ومن للتبعيض كما قال علم الهدى الشيخ أبو منصور الماتريدي في التأويلات لا للتبيين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas identifies the intended people of the Book as Jews around Medina: Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir, and Banu Qaynuqa.
rows.anchor: ما روي عن ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما من أن المراد بأهل الكتاب اليهود

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Another view denies that explanatory min entails all were unbelievers before the mission, since 'those who disbelieved' could describe their state after the mission.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض لا نسلم أن التبيين يقتضي كفر جميعهم قبل البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists are those who assign a partner to God, whether an idol or something else.
rows.anchor: وهم من اعتقدوا لله سبحانه شريكاً صنماً أو غيره

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Some restrict the intended polytheists to idol worshippers, since that described Arab polytheists around Mecca and Medina; this is attributed to Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وخصهم بعض بعبدة الأصنام لأن مشركي العرب الذين بمكة والمدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists are coordinated with Ahl al-Kitab; partitive min does not require some of the combined group to be non-disbelievers, since it can qualify a subset of the whole.
rows.anchor: فالعطف على أهل الكتاب ولا يلزم على التبعيض أن لا يكون بعضهم كافرين

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: An interpretation including the people of the Book among polytheists because they call Christ or Ezra God's son, coordinated only by label, is rejected as untenable.
rows.anchor: واحتمال أن يراد بالمشركين أهل الكتاب وشركهم لقولهم المسيح ابن الله

rows.speaker: قارئ
rows.claim: A variant reads al-mushrikūna in the nominative, coordinated with the relative pronoun; the majority accusative form cannot be explained as a genitive by adjacency.
rows.anchor: وقرئ والمشركون بالرفع عطفاً على الموصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prepositional phrase min ahl al-kitab functions circumstantially with the pronoun in kafaru.
rows.anchor: والجار والمجرور في موضع الحال من ضمير كفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Infikak originally means separation of things joined together; here munfakkin means parting from the state they held, as explained later.
rows.anchor: والانفكاك في الأصل افتراق الأمور الملتحمة بنوع مزايلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Munfakkin is yakun's predicate and an active participle from complete intransitive انفك; one grammarian instead supplies an omitted predicate from the deficient verb, which Al-Ālūsī criticizes as impermissible without necessity.
rows.anchor: فالوصف اسم فاعل من انفك التامة دون الناقصة الداخلة على المبتدأ والخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The until-clause attaches to munfakkin; bayyina can mean one who clarifies truth or the familiar proof establishing a claim, here a miracle.
rows.anchor: متعلق بمنفكين والبينة صفة بمعنى اسم الفاعل أي المبين للحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rasūl is either a complete apposition to al-bayyina or the predicate of an omitted subject meaning 'it is a Messenger'; its indefinite form magnifies him, and min Allah adds grandeur.
rows.anchor: بدل منها بدل كل من كل أو خبر لمقدر أي هي رسول وتنوينه للتفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'from God' modifies Messenger and adds honor by relation, reinforcing the grandeur inherent in the indefinite noun.
rows.anchor: في موضع الصفة له مفيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recitation clause is either another adjective of Messenger or a circumstantial clause attached to the pronoun in the first adjective.
rows.anchor: صفة أخرى له أو حال من الضمير في صفته الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase in the pages is a second adjective of ṣuḥuf or a circumstantial clause linked to the pronoun in muṭahhara; alternatively, only the prepositional phrase modifies, with kutub as its subject.
rows.anchor: صفة ثانية لصحفاً أو حال من الضمير في صفتها الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If bayyina means the Prophet who clarifies truth, identifying the proof with him is straightforward; if it means proof, his qualities are miraculous, as al-Ghazali and al-Busiri indicate, alongside other manifest miracles.
rows.anchor: وإطلاق البينة عليه عليه الصلاة والسلام على المعنى الأول ظاهر وعلى المعنى الأخير باعتبار أن أخلاقه وصفاته

rows.speaker: قتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: Qatada and Ibn Zayd are reported to take al-bayyina as the Qur'an, because it clarifies truth or is a miraculous proof establishing the claim.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بالبينة القرآن لأنه مبين للحق أو معجز مثبت للمدعي وروي ذلك عن قتادة وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If bayyina means Qur'an, rasūl may be an apposition with an omitted noun such as proof, revelation, miracle, or book of a Messenger, or a predicate with such a noun understood.
rows.anchor: عليه قيل بدل اشتمال أو بدل كل من كل أيضاً بتقدير مضاف أي بينة أو وحي أو معجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses make rasūl the subject with yatlū as predicate, explaining al-bayyina, interrupting to praise it, or modifying al-bayyina understood as the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون رسول مبتدأ لوصفه وخبره جملة

rows.speaker: أبي وعبد الله
rows.claim: Ubayy and Abdullah read rasūlan in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative from al-bayyina.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي وعبد الله رسولاً بالنصب على الحالية من البينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣuḥuf is a plural of ṣaḥīfa, like ṣuḥāf, meaning writing sheets; its root conveys something spread out.
rows.anchor: والصحف جمع صحيفة وكذا الصحاف القراطيس التي يكتب فيها وأصلها المبسوط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purified may mean protected from falsehood by explicit metaphor, or pages touched only by ritually pure people, with the attribution made figuratively.
rows.anchor: والمراد بتطهيرها تنزيهها عن الباطل على سبيل الاستعارة المصرحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kutub means written contents and qayyima means upright, speaking truth. Al-Taysir says these are the prophets' books, confirmed by the Qur'an as though contained within it.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالكتب المكتوبات وبالقيمة المستقيمة واستقامتها نطقها بالحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Prophet famously neither read nor wrote, saying he recites the pages transfers the action to its object: by reciting their contents it is as if he read the sheets.
rows.anchor: بناء على المشهور من أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام لم يكن يقرأ الكتاب كما أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم لم يكن يكتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations posit an omitted 'like' before pages, an implicit metaphor comparing the Prophet to a reader of their contents, or ṣuḥuf as a metonym for contents.
rows.anchor: وقيل على تقدير مضاف أي مثل صحف وقيل في ضمير يتلو استعارة مكنية

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Some take the Messenger as Gabriel and the purified pages as angelic copies from the Preserved Tablet; Al-Ālūsī rejects this and prefers Muhammad, as reported from Ibn Abbas, Muqatil, and others.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بالرسول جبريل عليه السلام وبالصحف صحف الملائكة عليهم السلام المنتسخة من اللوح المحفوظ

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi calls this one of the Qur'an's hardest passages in syntax and interpretation: if both groups disbelieved before the mission, the apparent sense says the Messenger's arrival ended their disbelief, contrary to history and 98:4, which says the people of the Book split only after the proof came.
rows.anchor: حتى قال الواحدي في كتاب البسيط أنها من أصعب ما في القرآن نظماً وتفسيراً
